title: CedarPoint technical deep dive: content guardrails performance options
summary: Deep technical discussion about where to place content guardrails (pre-filter client-side, inline GPU filter, async post-filter, or hybrid) and the performance cost of each approach. Covered KV cache/batching interactions, quantization impacts on safety models, VPC/on-prem constraints, and suggested pilot benchmarks and success metrics.
action_items: Sophie Chen - send detailed perf spreadsheet comparing inline vs async filter (p50/p95/p99) - due 2025-07-25
Marcus Valdez - run 3 benchmark configs on Redwood Dedicated replica with KV caching toggled - due 2025-07-28
Ethan Cole - provide sample production prompts and expected throughput envelope - due 2025-07-22
Marta Silva - share security checklist and required compliance docs - due 2025-07-24
next_steps: Redwood to share performance spreadsheet and recommended configs
Customer to provide sample prompt corpus + traffic shape
Schedule pilot run on Dedicated or Private for full-stack latency measurements
Follow-up meeting to review benchmark results w/ logs and token-level traces
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Valdez (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (CedarPoint VP Eng), Ethan Cole (Platform Lead), Marta Silva (Security Architect)

[00:00] Sophie: ok hi everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Sophie from Redwood, I'll hand off to Marcus for the deep dive.
[00:18] Marcus: yeah hi all, thanks, uh quick agenda — we wanna map out where guardrails can live in your stack and what latency and cost looks like for each option. I'll sketch 4 patterns and then we'll go into benching.
[00:30] Ethan: sounds good, we're particularly sensitive to p95 latency and also the idea of keeping PHI in-proc, so VPC or on-prem matters.
[00:40] Marta: and for us security is primary — we need audit logs, KMS-integrated keys, SSO, and SOC2 evidence. But we also can't blow latency for patient-facing flows.
[00:52] Marcus: totally. pattern A: client-side pre-filter. cheap, removes obvious bad content before it hits inference, zero GPU cycles — but it's best-effort and can leak prompt variants to client logic.
[01:10] Priya: quick question, client-side means we'd run some JS or microservice inside our network?
[01:15] Marcus: yeah either client code or an in-house microservice in your VPC — basically a lightweight classifier on CPU. fast but less accurate than model-based safety.
[01:24] Sophie: noted that tends to reduce volume to the LLM and lowers cost but can't be your only control for nuanced medical content.
[01:33] Marcus: pattern B: inline synchronous safety model — run a small safety model as a pre-step on the GPU path, ideally quantized so it co-resides with the main model and can block or transform outputs before streaming. This adds on-path latency but avoids sending content elsewhere.
[01:53] Ethan: what's the p95 hit for that? ballpark numbers?
[01:58] Marcus: depends on model size and quantization. example: a 1B-safety model on GPU quantized to int8 might add ~15-40 ms on top of generation for short prompts if run as fused op; on CPU it could be 150-300 ms. With batching sometimes the incremental cost amortizes, but for low-latency requests it shows up.
[02:20] Marta: 15-40 ms is ok, but if users need streaming tokens we worry about head-of-line blocking.
[02:28] Marcus: yes — placement matters for streaming. If safety is synchronous pre-generation you may delay start of tokens. One hybrid is to allow early token streaming while running a fast filter in parllel and retract/flag as needed — but that needs client support for retraction.
[02:45] Priya: oh retraction is messy for UX.
[02:48] Marcus: agreed. pattern C: async post-filter — generate, stream, and then run safety check post-hoc. pros: minimal on-path latency; cons: you may have already delivered content and must do remediation flows. works well when you can do limited retroactive actions (moderation logs, follow-up corrections).
[03:05] Sophie: and pattern D is hybrid routing — run a quick cheap filter inline and escalate ambiguous cases to a heavier model or human-in-the-loop out-of-band.
[03:15] Ethan: ok, how does KV cache interact? we use prefix-heavy prompts with patient templates.
[03:20] Marcus: KV cache reduces generation work for repeated prefixes; however, if safety runs as a separate model per request you might lose some of that amortization. two common approaches: share KV cache across models (if compatible) or run safety on the same runtime to reuse cache. sharing requires model architecture alignment — often not trivial.
[03:40] Marta: meaning we'd have to use the same tokenizer and same model family?
[03:44] Marcus: exactly. or you maintain a separate safety KV that captures prefix state for safety runs — extra storage and complexity. Also batching plays into this: large batches improve GPU throughput but increase tail latency for individual requests.
[03:58] Priya: can we change batching config dynamically per route? e.g., patient-facing route with small batch/low latency and internal summarization route with big batch?
[04:06] Marcus: yes, Redwood routing supports per-route batching policies and SLO-driven scheduling; you can set max latency thresholds and Redwood will avoid batching beyond that window.
[04:15] Ethan: quantization — does quantizing the safety model make classification worse?
[04:20] Marcus: it can. quantization to int8 typically preserves classification accuracy well for many safety models but edge-cases exist. we recommend A/B tests: run quantized safety alongside float baseline and compare false positives/negatives on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles.
[04:38] Marta: for compliance, we need audit logs of decisions. if safety runs in a separate service, how do we maintain consistent logging?
[04:44] Sophie: Redwood can emit token-level traces and per-decision audit entries; if you route to private deployment we can push logs to your SIEM or S3 with KMS.
[04:52] Marcus: important detail — if safety runs outside your VPC you must consider data residency and export controls; for CedarPoint you probably want Private or Dedicated with VPC.
[05:04] Priya: yep leaning Private. what's the perf delta for on-prem vs our hosted Dedicated?
[05:10] Marcus: depends on hardware. on-prem with equivalently provisioned GPUs will be similar; the difference is network overhead and operator maintenance. Dedicated in-cloud can offer more predictable autoscaling. For ultra-low latency colocated with app servers, on-prem can shave maybe 10-30 ms of network RTT.
[05:28] Ethan: can safety be offloaded to CPU to save GPU cycles?
[05:31] Marcus: yes, many teams run safety classifiers on CPU if the model is small enough — saves GPU cost but adds latency. There's also a middle-ground: a tiny CPU pre-filter + GPU secondary check for ambiguous cases.
[05:45] Marta: for patient flows we can't accept false negatives. Are ensembles recommended?
[05:50] Marcus: ensembles increase cost but help recall — e.g., run cheap filter then a more expensive specialized safety model. Another pattern is thresholding: use a conservative cheap filter to catch most bad content then escalate. We'll need your acceptable FNR/FPR tradeoff.
[06:05] Priya: let's talk numbers — we'd like p95 end-to-end under 300ms for interactive triage, and cost per request below $0.02 normalized.
[06:14] Sophie: good anchors. Marcus, can you outline which configuration hits both?
[06:18] Marcus: high-level — option 1 (client pre-filter + async post-filter): p95 can be ~120-200 ms since filter is local, generation unchanged, but remediation cost exists. CPU pre-filter keeps cost low. Option 2 (inline quantized safety on GPU): p95 might be 200-350 ms depending on model size and batching settings. Option 3 (hybrid tiny inline + escalations): you can get p95 ~150-250 ms while keeping false negatives low. These are ballpark and we should bench with your prompt set.
[06:48] Ethan: benching — what workload shape do you need? concurrency, token lengths, prompt patterns?
[06:53] Marcus: ideally: sample of 2k representative prompts, expected qps (peak and steady), token output distribution (avg/95/99 lengths), and any routing rules. We'll run tests with KV cache enabled/disabled and several batching windows (8ms, 16ms, 32ms).
[07:12] Marta: on the topic of streaming — if we stream tokens, how do we ensure safety without horrid UX?
[07:18] Marcus: three choices: put safety before streaming (adds start latency), stream optimistically then patch (UX jarring), or stream with progressive checks that only allow tokens with low-safety-risk to flow. The last requires partial-decoder scoring and small lookahead safety model; it's complex but lower latency.
[07:40] Sophie: note that partial-decoder checks sometimes interact poorly with KV caching because you can't always reuse prefix KVs if you run lookahead on a different model.
[07:52] Priya: for our clinicians, retraction is unacceptable. So we need a solution that prevents unsafe outputs at generation time. That suggests inline or hybrid conservative-first approach.
[08:03] Marcus: understood. then inline quantized safety or hybrid with conservative cheap filter inline will be the path.
[08:10] Ethan: does Redwood support running separate safety models on dedicated small GPUs to avoid head-of-line blocking for main generation GPUs?
[08:18] Marcus: yes, you can dedicate small GPU pools for safety. Redwood routing can send safety workloads to those pools to avoid interfering with generation throughput. That increases infra cost but isolates latency impact.
[08:30] Marta: when you say small GPU pools, are we talking T4s or A10s?
[08:35] Marcus: T4 or A10 is common for small models. For quantized int8 you can even run some safety models on CPU with optimized kernels but again latency tradeoffs.
[08:46] Priya: what's the operational complexity for us if we pick Private deployment? we have limited SRE bandwidth.
[08:52] Sophie: Private includes a customer-managed control plane but Redwood offers managed ops for the inference runtime as an add-on. We can run the pilot with Redwood-managed infra inside your VPC to reduce ops burden.
[09:04] Ethan: good. let's dig into KV cache specifics — if we do hybrid inline safety, can we keep a shared KV across safety and gen to reuse prefix states?
[09:13] Marcus: you can if the safety model is the same architecture and tokenization; otherwise you'd need conversion layers. Another pattern is keeping a synchronized prefix fingerprint to quickly reconstruct or rehydrate KV for safety runs. Synchronous rehydration can add 5-20 ms.
[09:31] Sophie: there's also cache eviction policies to consider — patient templates may be long and push out other KVs. We recommend LRU with pinning for high-value prefixes.
[09:39] Marta: any known gotchas with batching on private networks?
[09:43] Marcus: batching behavior is the same, but network jitter and ticketing between local app and inference can affect batching window heuristics. Also, when using autoscaling, cold-starts may affect tail latency if new pods are unprovisioned.
[09:57] Priya: can Redwood do warm-pools for critical routes?
[10:00] Marcus: yes, reserved warm capacity and provisioned dedicated pools are supported — that's what Redwood Dedicated is for.
[10:06] Ethan: on quantization regression tests — what's a practical A/B test setup?
[10:10] Marcus: run the quantized safety model in shadow mode for 2 weeks on production traffic (or on a sampled corpus) and compare decisions to float baseline. Track precision/recall on labelled examples and flag divergences for triage. Redwood Optimize helps automate that eval.
[10:26] Sophie: add to action items: we'll share the Optimize guide and the perf spreadsheet.
[10:30] Marcus: also to mention, if you use function/tool calling or structured outputs, safety checks sometimes need to run on both prompt and tool output; factor that into latency budget.
[10:43] Priya: our call flow uses tool calls for database lookups, so double-checking outputs is relevant.
[10:49] Marcus: right, so treat tool outputs as additional model outputs to moderate if they flow to users.
[10:55] Ethan: any differences in behavior for larger safety models (e.g. 7B) vs tiny 100M classifiers?
[11:02] Marcus: large safety models give better nuance but cost more and add latency. Tiny classifiers are fast but brittle. Many enterprise setups use a fast conservative classifier inline and send edge cases to a 1B-3B safety model offline or for escalation.
[11:18] Marta: for auditability we need model-versioned decisions with checksums, how does Redwood surface that?
[11:24] Marcus: every decision can include model_id, model_version, quant_profile, and a salted hash of the prompt and decision. We also stream these as structured log events to your audit sink.
[11:34] Sophie: slightly off topic — we should think about throttling/backpressure when safety escalations spike; Redwood supports backpressure policies and can return 429 or queued responses.
[11:45] Priya: queued responses are ok if we can keep p95 SLA.
[11:49] Marcus: one more note on ensemble costs — if you run multiple models per request you multiply token compute. Caching and batching must be tuned to avoid runaway costs.
[12:00] Ethan: earlier you mentioned kernel selection — is there any micro-optimization that helps safety models run faster?
[12:06] Marcus: yes — mixed precision, kernel fusion, attention optimizations, and quantization-specific kernels help. Redwood's runtime selects kernels based on model architecture and sequence length distribution. For safety models with short contexts, optimized small-seq kernels help a lot.
[12:20] Marta: do we need to do anything special with our prompts to avoid triggering chain-of-thought style hallucinations that safety models misclassify?
[12:28] Marcus: prompt engineering matters. You can preface prompts with system-level guardrail text and provide examples. Also include safety-specific instruction tokens. But don't over-prompt to avoid reducing utility.
[12:38] Priya: ok, let's go scenario-by-scenario for the pilot. Marcus?
[12:42] Marcus: propose three pilots:
[12:45] - Pilot A: Private deployment, inline tiny CPU pre-filter + GPU quantized safety inline on dedicated small GPU pool; measure p50/p95/p99, false neg/pos on labelled set.
[12:58] - Pilot B: Dedicated (cloud) with client pre-filter + async post-filter (saves GPU cycles) — measure remediation latency and cost per incident.
[13:08] - Pilot C: Hybrid streaming with progressive checks and pinning KV for frequently used prefixes — advanced, more infra complexity, measure UX metrics.
[13:19] Priya: Pilot A seems closest to our needs, but we'd like Pilot B as a low-cost baseline.
[13:25] Marcus: perfect. we'll scope Pilot A as the main track.
[13:29] Ethan: how long does a pilot typically take?
[13:32] Marcus: benching + config tuning is ~2 weeks, then a 2-4 week shadow run on sampled traffic, then rollout. So roughly 6 weeks to go from kickoff to initial rollout.
[13:44] Marta: what logs will we get during pilot?
[13:47] Sophie: token-level traces (optional), per-request latency breakdowns, model decision logs, and aggregated metrics. We'll redact PHI as requested or keep logs inside your VPC.
[13:59] Priya: what's the expected cost delta for Pilot A vs Pilot B?
[14:04] Marcus: Pilot A (inline quantized) will be more expensive per request than B because of on-path GPU checks — maybe 20-40% higher compute cost, but lower remediation overhead. Pilot B saves compute but incurs human/manual remediation cost if false negatives downstream.
[14:20] Ethan: do you have sample perf spreadsheet numbers?
[14:23] Marcus: yes we'll send one — it'll show scenario comparisons with p50/p95 and cost per 1M requests.
[14:30] Priya: let's talk about failure modes — how do we fail safe?
[14:34] Marcus: fail closed vs fail open decisions need to be explicit. For CedarPoint, I'd recommend fail-closed for anything ambiguous in patient-facing flows and route ambiguous cases to a human queue. Redwood supports policy flags to control default behavior.
[14:47] Marta: for compliance we need the ability to produce a decision trail for any flagged output.
[14:52] Sophie: Redwood stores per-decision metadata and you can export those logs on demand.
[14:57] Ethan: quick Q on adaptive batching — can you turn batching off during peak events or for particular customers?
[15:03] Marcus: yes, Redwood supports per-customer and per-route policies; you can set batching windows and priority levels.
[15:09] Priya: do you support hardware-level isolation for dedicated customers?
[15:13] Marcus: yes, Dedicated capacity can be single-tenant pools. For Private on-prem you control node tenancy.
[15:20] Marta: anything special about encryption or KMS when safety runs inside our VPC?
[15:25] Marcus: we support bringing your own KMS and hardware HSM integrations for key management. Logs can be encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys.
[15:33] Ethan: for the bench runs, do you need us to provide test harness or will Redwood run using our traffic replay?
[15:38] Marcus: either works. if you provide traffic replay it's ideal — we can also instrument our harness to mimic it. We'll need the prompt corpus and token length distribution.
[15:48] Priya: we'll send samples and traffic shapes.
[15:50] Sophie: noted.
[15:52] Marcus: a few more nuanced notes: 1) If you plan to do on-device client-side filtering for mobile clients, consider differential models per platform due to compute constraints. 2) For streaming, ensure client tolerates partial results if you use optimistic streaming. 3) If you enforce regulatory redaction, put redaction rules before any telemetry exfil.
[16:16] Priya: about redaction — can Redwood redact tokens from logs before they leave VPC?
[16:20] Marcus: yes, we can apply regex or model-based redaction and ensure redacted logs only contain non-PHI. We'll coordinate with Marta on patterns.
[16:31] Marta: thanks. can you also show us how policy updates roll out? we need to be able to update safety rules quickly and roll back.
[16:38] Marcus: policy rollouts are versioned and can be canaryed by percentage. You can pin a route to a policy version. Rollback is a single API call.
[16:46] Ethan: any differences if we use OpenAI or other vendor for safety vs Redwood's hosted/embedded models?
[16:51] Marcus: using external vendor adds network hops and concerns about data residency. Also, you'd have less kernel/runtime control and harder integration with KV cache and batching. OpenGuard/ServiceX were mentioned as competitors but they typically operate as separate filter services.
[17:04] Priya: ok good to know.
[17:06] Marcus: let me run through a recommended config for Pilot A: Private VPC with one small GPU pool for gen (A10x2), one dedicated T4 pool for safety models, KV caching with pinned prefixes for templates, batching window 8ms for interactive route, quantized int8 safety model (1B) inline, conservative pre-filter on CPU. We'll document exact CPU/GPU sizes in the spreadsheet.
[17:31] Sophie: we'll include cost estimates and ops overhead.
[17:35] Marta: on incident response — if safety model misclassifies something high-severity, can we trigger a kill-switch to block further responses?
[17:41] Marcus: yes, there's a global policy toggle you can call via API or through the Console to set routes to fail-closed or pause. It can integrate with your incident management.
[17:51] Ethan: one more thought — could we instrument per-user adaptation without leaking PHI? like personalize but keep it safe?
[17:58] Marcus: personalization at inference time is possible via per-user KVs but storing PHI must follow your compliance guidelines; we support encryption and strict access controls. For safety, you would avoid storing raw PHI in logs.
[18:10] Priya: we're happy to send sample prompts tonight.
[18:13] Sophie: great. Marcus, any final run-down?
[18:16] Marcus: final checklist: 1) we run bench matrix (inline quantized vs async vs hybrid), 2) we'll include KV enabled/disabled, batching windows 8/16/32ms, 3) safety model quant profiles to A/B, 4) telemetry and audit config, 5) run 2-week shadow run on sampled traffic.
[18:35] Priya: timeline works.
[18:37] Marta: thanks.
[18:39] Sophie: ok wrapping — we'll send the perf spreadsheet, Optimize guide, and security docs. Meet again after we have bench results.
[18:46] Ethan: thanks everyone.
[18:48] Marcus: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
